::: {.callout-tip}
## What a budget is for

An uncertainty budget is not a formality at the end of a report. It is the
only part of the report that tells the reader what the result is worth, and
the only part that tells *you* what to improve next. A measurement without one
is an opinion with decimals.
:::

Every AMLab experiment ends with the same construction, following the GUM
[@gum2008].

**1. Write the model.** State the measurand $Y$ as a function of the
quantities you actually observed,
$Y = f(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_N)$. If you cannot write the function you cannot
build the budget, and usually you have not understood the measurement.

**2. List the input quantities.** Everything that enters $f$, plus everything
that affects the result without appearing in $f$ — the influence quantities.
The second group is where budgets go wrong: ambient temperature, the host
operating system, self-heating, the loading of a divider by the input it
drives.

**3. Evaluate each standard uncertainty.** A **Type A** evaluation comes from
the statistics of repeated observations, most often $s/\sqrt{n}$. A **Type B**
evaluation comes from anything else: an instrument specification, a
calibration certificate, a datasheet bound, physical reasoning. The
distinction is about *how you found the number*, not about its quality — a
Type B component is not a lesser one.

For a Type B bound of half-width $a$:

| What you know | Distribution | $u(x_i)$ |
|---|---|---|
| A certificate quoting $U$ with $k$ | Normal | $U/k$ |
| A bound, nothing about the inside | Rectangular | $a/\sqrt{3}$ |
| A bound, values near the centre more likely | Triangular | $a/\sqrt{6}$ |
| A sinusoidal variation of amplitude $a$ | U-shaped | $a/\sqrt{2}$ |

: Type B evaluations {#tbl-typeb}

**4. Compute the sensitivity coefficients.**
$c_i = \partial f/\partial X_i$, evaluated at the operating point. A
sensitivity coefficient carries units, and getting it wrong is the most common
way to produce a budget that is internally consistent and physically
meaningless.

**5. Combine.** With uncorrelated inputs,

$$
u_c(y) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(c_i\,u(x_i)\right)^2}
$$ {#eq-uc-shared}

**6. Expand.** $U = k\,u_c$, with $k = 2$ for a coverage probability of
approximately 95 % when the combined distribution is approximately normal.
Always say which $k$ you used; a number quoted without it is unusable.

**7. Read the budget.** The index
$h_i = (c_i u(x_i))^2 / u_c^2$ says what fraction of the variance each
component holds. Report it. The component with the largest index is the only
one worth spending money or time on, and the components below a few per cent
can be improved indefinitely with no effect at all.

`labtools`' `budget_table()` performs steps 3, 5, 6 and 7 from a list of
components; steps 1, 2 and 4 are yours, and they are the ones that require
understanding the measurement.
